what_happened.summary: Striking out to end the game is tough, and it’s okay if he feels upset. The ball-strike calls were the umpire’s judgment, so whether those pitches were outside isn’t something to argue or protest. One at-bat is just information; what matters is his readiness, approach and effort, not the result. This guidance comes from draft coaching notes that haven’t been reviewed yet.

output.call_type_rationale: The strikeout depended on the umpire’s ball/strike calls, which are judgment calls and cannot be protested or reviewed; no written rule determines the outcome or answers the parent’s question about mental resilience.

channel.who: You as the parent, with the head coach handling any technique later
channel.how: On the ride home or at a calm time later, let him speak first, say “I love watching you play,” praise his effort and approach, and avoid breaking down what went wrong unless he asks

output.teachable_moment: A strikeout is one at-bat of information, not a measure of his worth; he can learn from it and still be a great teammate and person.

individual: Practice the two-strike approach off a tee: from a tee on the outer half, use a slightly shorter two-strike swing and drive the ball the other way, five quality reps, helmet on, net set so missed balls stay clear of walkways.
team: Coach runs a short two-strike situational drill so hitters practice protecting the plate and resetting between pitches.
at_home: Let him lead the conversation after games; say “I love watching you play” and praise effort and approach rather than critiquing the strikeout.

output.focus: Let him speak first on the ride home; say 'I love watching you play' and praise his effort.

life_lesson.text: Your son’s value isn’t defined by a stat line or one game-ending out; even great hitters fail most of the time. Beyond baseball, what matters is how he responds to setbacks and keeps showing up with effort.

lessons.title: Your value isn't your stat line
lessons.principle: Your value is not determined by your failures or your successes.

lessons.title: A game built on failure
lessons.principle: In baseball, succeeding about 30% of the time at the plate can make a Hall of Fame career at the professional level. That's a 70% failure rate. You will not win every competition, and you will not lose every competition, but you will learn and grow through every competition.

recalled.content: Coach wants to know if the pitcher can pitch Sunday

2026-10-18: a coach asked about Little League pitch count rest eligibility for a 12U pitcher after throwing 68 pitches. Focus given: Develop other pitchers for Sunday and follow the 5-day rest rule. Lesson: Winning comes from a winning formula; Believe in your players before they believe in themselves. Pitcher eligible again 2026-10-22.
